headline: State desk: Connecticut sets sales record; Rhode Island tops $102M
dek: Connecticut adult-use sales hit a record $20.5 million in October as prices fell to $6.36 a gram; Rhode Island passed $102 million through October.
key_points: Connecticut's adult-use sales reached $20,482,897 in October, beating December 2025's record by about $378,000, in the first month of its new flat tax.
The average Connecticut gram fell to $6.36, down 24.6% in a year and 43.3% in two.
Rhode Island's sales reached $102.3 million through October; the year-to-date pace points to a record year above 2025's $120.1 million.
Portland, Oregon's mayor proposed removing a city ban on drive-through and walk-up cannabis windows and raising the deferred licence fee down payment to 50%.
body: Two New England markets reported October numbers on 10 November that tell the same story from different angles: more product moving at lower prices. In Oregon, Portland's mayor brought a clean-up of the city's cannabis code to committee. Here is the state desk for the evening.
## Connecticut: a record month under a new tax

Connecticut's licensed retailers sold $20,482,897 of adult-use cannabis in October, a new monthly record, according to Department of Consumer Protection figures reported by The Marijuana Herald. The previous high was $20,104,680 in December 2025, so October beat it by about $378,000, or 1.9%. Medical sales added $5,287,794, bringing the month to $25,770,691; combined sales still fell just short of December 2025's $26.06 million.

Through ten months, Connecticut has sold about $245.8 million, of which $191.3 million was adult-use and $54.5 million medical. Adult-use sales were up about 7.9% on October 2025 and combined sales about 4.5%. Medical sales continue to shrink: October's figure was about 6.9% below the $5.68 million recorded a year earlier, by MetaFlora's comparison with the state's monthly series.

Price is doing the work. The average price of a gram fell to $6.36 in October, a record low, from $8.43 a year earlier and $11.21 in October 2024: a 24.6% drop in one year and 43.3% in two. Paybotic's analysis of September data showed the same pattern, with stores selling 30% more products than a year earlier at an 18% lower average price per item.

October was also the first full month under Connecticut's new tax. Public Act 26-68 replaced the THC-based excise tax with a flat 10.75% tax on gross receipts from 1 October, which with the 6.35% sales tax and 3% municipal tax takes the total on adult-use purchases to 20.1%, according to Paybotic. One month is too early to credit the record to the tax change, which removed the potency-based charge on stronger products.
> Connecticut is selling more cannabis than ever for less money per gram. Record months now come from volume, not price.
## Rhode Island: on course for a record year

Rhode Island's retailers sold $102,263,919 of cannabis in the first ten months of 2026, including $10.56 million in October, according to Cannabis Control Commission data reported by The Marijuana Herald. October's adult-use sales were about $9.53 million and medical sales about $1.03 million; the month was 1.7% above October 2025.

Monthly sales have stayed in a narrow band all year, from $9.32 million in February to a record $10.81 million in July, which the commission's annual report confirmed as the state's best month. At the year-to-date average of about $10.2 million a month, November and December would add roughly $20.5 million, taking 2026 to about $122.7 million, above 2025's $120.1 million. Retailers need about $17.8 million to set the record.

Pre-packaged flower led product sales at about $40.3 million through October, followed by raw pre-rolls at $21.6 million, vape cartridges at $17.7 million and edibles at $11.7 million. Wholesale transfers between licensees reached $43.9 million, 23% of them between affiliated businesses. The state counted 6,605 active medical patients in October.
## Portland, Oregon: code catches up with state rules

Portland Mayor Keith Wilson introduced Ordinance 2026-407, which the City Council's City Life Committee took up on 10 November, to amend the city's cannabis licensing code, Chapter 14B.130. It would strike a city ban on drive-through and walk-up windows built into licensed shops, a restriction the Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission relaxed in 2020, first temporarily and then in permanent rules allowing on-site delivery, according to the city's ordinance page. Sales from temporary structures, carts or satellite sites would remain banned, The Marijuana Herald reported.

The ordinance also tightens the city's Deferred Payment Program, which lets licensees spread the $3,970 annual fee. The down payment rises from $600 under the old code to 50% of the fee, or $1,985 today, with the rest due within six months, and a second late fee charged at 60 days is removed. The city says about 31% of licensees use the programme and that it has seen significant misuse; the changes have been applied since August and the ordinance writes them into code.

Connecticut's November data will show whether October's record holds as the flat tax settles in; watch medical sales, which keep falling. Rhode Island needs about $17.8 million over the last two months for a record year. Portland's ordinance goes from committee to the full City Council.
